〔委託元となるお客様の商号〕（以下「委託元」という。）と{{COMPANY}}（以下「委託先」という。）は、委託元が{{PRODUCT}}（以下「本サービス」という。）を利用するにあたり、委託元が委託先に対して個人データの取扱いを委託することに関し、次のとおり個人データの取扱いに関する覚書（以下「本覚書」という。）を締結する。 # 第1章 総則 # 第1条（目的及び適用範囲） 本覚書は、委託元が本サービスの利用に伴い委託先に取り扱わせる個人データについて、個人情報保護法その他の関係法令を遵守した取扱いを確保するため、委託元及び委託先の権利義務を定めることを目的とする。 委託元が委託先に対して個人データを提供し、委託先がこれを取り扱う行為は、個人情報保護法第27条第5項第1号に定める委託に伴う提供に該当し、同条第1項の第三者提供には該当しないことを、両当事者は確認する。 本覚書は、委託元と委託先との間の 利用規約 その他本サービスの提供に関する契約（以下「本契約」という。）の一部を構成する。 個人データの取扱いに関する事項について本覚書の定めと本契約の定めとが抵触する場合には、本覚書の定めが優先して適用されるものとする。それ以外の事項については本契約の定めによる。 本覚書は、委託元が本サービスにおいて取り扱う個人データのうち、委託元が個人情報取扱事業者として取り扱うものに適用する。委託先が自らの事業のために取得し、自ら利用目的を定めて取り扱う個人情報（委託元の担当者の氏名及び連絡先、課金及び請求に関する情報、サービスの稼働状況に関する情報等）については、本覚書は適用されず、委託先の プライバシーポリシー の定めるところによる。 法令 個人情報保護法 第27条第5項第1号（第三者提供の制限） 利用目的の達成に必要な範囲内において個人データの取扱いの全部または一部を委託することに伴って個人データが提供される場合、その提供を受ける者は「第三者」に該当しないものとされています。このため、委託に基づく提供については本人の同意を得る必要がありません。一方で、委託元には同法第25条に基づく委託先の監督義務が生じ、委託先は委託された業務の範囲を超えて個人データを取り扱うことができません。 # 第2条（定義） 本覚書において使用する用語の意義は、次の各号に定めるところによる。本覚書で定義しない用語は、個人情報保護法及び本契約の定めるところによる。 個人情報 個人情報保護法第2条第1項に定める個人情報をいう。生存する個人に関する情報であって、氏名その他の記述等（音声、動作その他の方法を用いて表された一切の事項を含む。）により特定の個人を識別することができるもの（他の情報と容易に照合することができ、それにより特定の個人を識別することができることとなるものを含む。）をいう。 個人データ 個人情報保護法第16条第3項に定める個人データ、すなわち個人情報データベース等を構成する個人情報をいう。 要配慮個人情報 個人情報保護法第2条第3項に定める要配慮個人情報をいう。本人の人種、信条、社会的身分、病歴、犯罪の経歴、犯罪により害を被った事実その他同法施行令第2条に定める記述等が含まれる個人情報をいう。 個人情報取扱事業者 個人情報保護法にいう個人情報取扱事業者をいう。 委託 個人情報保護法第27条第5項第1号にいう、利用目的の達成に必要な範囲内における個人データの取扱いの全部または一部の委託をいう。 委託元個人データ 委託元が本サービスの利用に伴い委託先に取り扱わせる個人データをいう。その具体的な項目、本人の範囲、取扱いの目的及び取扱期間は別紙1に定める。 再委託先 委託先が委託元個人データの取扱いの全部または一部を再委託する相手方をいう。再委託先がさらに委託する場合の相手方（再々委託先以下を含む。）を含む。 漏えい等 委託元個人データの漏えい、滅失または毀損をいい、これらが発生したおそれがある事態を含む。 安全管理措置 個人情報保護法第23条に基づき、個人データの漏えい等の防止その他の個人データの安全管理のために講ずる必要かつ適切な措置をいう。 本人 委託元個人データによって識別される特定の個人をいう。 法令 個人情報保護法 第2条第1項（定義）／第16条第3項（定義） 個人情報には、音声その他の方法を用いて表された一切の事項により特定の個人を識別できるものが含まれます。ガイドライン（通則編）は、本人の氏名が含まれる等の理由により特定の個人を識別できる音声録音情報を、個人情報に該当する事例として挙げています。本サービスで取り扱う会議の音声、文字起こし、ノート、話者名は、参加者の氏名やカレンダーの招待情報と容易に照合できるため、通常は個人情報に当たり、ワークスペース単位で検索できる形で保存される以上、個人データにも当たります。 # 第3条（委託の内容） 委託元は、委託先に対し、本サービスの提供を受けるために必要な範囲で、委託元個人データの取扱いを委託する。委託先はこれを受託する。 委託する業務の内容、取り扱う個人データの項目、本人の範囲、取扱いの目的及び取扱期間は、別紙1に定めるところによる。 委託元は、委託元個人データを委託先に提供するにあたり、その取得が個人情報保護法その他の法令に従って適正に行われたものであること、及び委託先による取扱いが委託元の特定した利用目的の達成に必要な範囲内であることを保証する。 委託元は、本サービスの利用にあたり、あらかじめ特定した利用目的の範囲を超えて委託元個人データが取り扱われることのないよう、自らの責任において利用目的の特定、通知または公表その他の必要な措置を講じるものとする。 委託元は、会議の記録にあたり、参加者に対して録音及び文字起こしが行われることを告知すること、並びに要配慮個人情報が記録される可能性がある場合に本人の同意を得ることについて、自らの責任において対応するものとする。 法令 個人情報保護法 第17条第1項（利用目的の特定）／第20条第1項（適正な取得）／第20条第2項（適正な取得） 個人情報の取扱いにあたっては利用目的をできる限り特定しなければならず、偽りその他不正の手段による取得は禁止されています。また、要配慮個人情報は、法令に基づく場合など限られた例外を除き、あらかじめ本人の同意を得ないで取得してはならないとされています。会議の記録において参加者への告知や本人の同意の取得を行う主体は、個人データの取扱いについて自ら利用目的を定める委託元です。 第3条第3項から第5項は、取得の適法性と本人への対応の責任が委託元にあることを定めるものである。参加者への告知の考え方と文例は AI議事録をどこまで使ってよいか（チーム向けガイド） に掲載している。 # 第2章 委託先の義務 # 第4条（委託元の指示に従った取扱い及び目的外利用の禁止） 委託先は、委託元個人データを、本契約、本覚書及び別紙1に定める範囲並びに委託元の指示に従ってのみ取り扱うものとし、これらの範囲を超えて取り扱ってはならない。 委託先は、委託元個人データを、委託された業務の遂行以外の目的に利用してはならない。委託先自身の事業のための分析、統計の作成、AIモデルの開発または改良を含め、委託の範囲を超える取扱いは行わないものとする。AIモデルの学習への利用については第14条に定める。 本契約及び本覚書は、委託元から委託先に対する個人データの取扱いに関する包括的な指示を構成する。本契約及び本覚書の範囲を超える個別の指示は、書面（電磁的記録を含む。以下同じ。）によるものとし、これに要する費用の負担について両当事者が別途合意するものとする。 委託先は、委託元の指示が個人情報保護法その他の法令に違反すると判断した場合には、遅滞なくその旨を委託元に通知するものとする。この場合、委託先は当該指示に従うことを拒むことができる。 委託先は、法令に基づき委託元個人データを取り扱う必要がある場合には、法令上禁止されている場合を除き、あらかじめその旨を委託元に通知するものとする。 法令 個人情報保護法 第18条第1項（利用目的による制限） 個人情報取扱事業者は、あらかじめ本人の同意を得ないで、特定された利用目的の達成に必要な範囲を超えて個人情報を取り扱ってはなりません。委託に伴って個人データの提供を受けた者は、委託された業務以外に当該個人データを取り扱うことはできないと、ガイドライン（通則編）は整理しています。第4条第1項及び第2項は、この制限を契約上の義務として定めたものです。委託元による監督については第9条の引用を参照してください。 # 第5条（第三者への開示の制限及び法令に基づく開示要請への対応） 委託先は、委託元の事前の書面による承諾なく、委託元個人データを第三者に提供し、または開示してはならない。ただし、第9条に定める再委託先に対する提供、及び次項の定めによる場合はこの限りでない。 委託先は、法令に基づく場合、または裁判所、捜査機関その他の権限を有する公的機関から適法かつ有効な要請を受けた場合に限り、必要な範囲で委託元個人データを開示することができる。 委託先は、前項の要請を受けた場合、法令上禁止されている場合及び緊急を要する場合を除き、開示に先立って委託元にその旨を通知し、委託元が不服申立てその他の対抗手段をとる機会を確保するものとする。 委託先は、前項の要請に対し、可能な限り、要請元に対して委託元に直接照会するよう求めるものとする。 委託先は、委託元個人データを、いかなる名目によっても販売してはならない。 # 第6条（安全管理措置） 委託先は、委託元個人データの漏えい等の防止その他の安全管理のために、個人情報保護法第23条に基づく必要かつ適切な措置を講じるものとする。 前項の措置の内容は、個人データの取扱いに関する基本方針の策定及び取扱規律の整備を前提として、組織的安全管理措置、人的安全管理措置、物理的安全管理措置、技術的安全管理措置並びに外的環境の把握の各区分について、別紙2に定めるところによる。 委託先は、技術の進展、脅威の変化及び業界の標準に応じて安全管理措置の内容を変更することができる。ただし、変更後の措置の水準が変更前の水準を実質的に下回るものであってはならない。 委託先は、外国において委託元個人データを取り扱う場合には、当該外国の個人情報の保護に関する制度を把握したうえで、安全管理のために必要かつ適切な措置を講じるものとする。委託先は、委託元の求めに応じて、当該外国の名称、サーバーの所在国の名称及び把握を踏まえて講じた措置の内容を委託元に提供するものとする。 委託元は、本サービスの利用にあたり、アカウントの認証情報及びAPIの認証情報の管理、自社内における利用権限の設定、並びに管理者による共有範囲の設定について、自らの責任において適切な措置を講じるものとする。 法令 個人情報保護法 第23条（安全管理措置）／第32条第1項第4号（保有個人データに関する事項の公表等） 個人情報取扱事業者は、個人データの漏えい、滅失または毀損の防止その他の個人データの安全管理のために必要かつ適切な措置を講じなければなりません。ガイドライン（通則編）別添は、この措置を基本方針の策定、取扱規律の整備、組織的安全管理措置、人的安全管理措置、物理的安全管理措置、技術的安全管理措置、外的環境の把握の7項目に整理しています。このうち外的環境の把握は、外国において個人データを取り扱う場合に、当該外国の個人情報の保護に関する制度等を把握したうえで必要かつ適切な措置を講じることを求めるものです。委託元が同法第32条第1項第4号及び同法施行令第10条第1号に基づいて講じた措置の内容を公表するにあたり、第6条第4項の情報提供はその前提となります。 # 第7条（従業者の監督及び秘密保持） 委託先は、委託元個人データを取り扱う従業者に対し、個人情報保護法第24条に基づく必要かつ適切な監督を行うものとする。 委託先は、委託元個人データを取り扱う従業者の範囲を業務上必要な限度に限定し、当該従業者との間で秘密保持に関する義務を定めるものとする。この義務は、当該従業者の退職後も存続する。 委託先は、委託元個人データを取り扱う従業者に対し、個人データの取扱いに関する教育を、就業の開始時及び定期的に実施するものとする。 委託先は、本覚書に基づいて知り得た委託元の秘密情報及び委託元個人データを、本覚書の目的以外に使用せず、第三者に開示または漏えいしてはならない。本項の義務は、本覚書の終了後も存続する。 本サービスのうち利用者間のやり取りを媒介する機能に関して委託先が知り得た通信の秘密に属する情報について、委託先及びその従業者は、法令に基づく場合その他の正当な理由がある場合を除き、これを取得し、利用し、または開示しない。この義務は在職中及び退職後を通じて継続する。 法令 電気通信事業法 第4条（秘密の保護）／第179条（罰則） 電気通信事業者の取扱中に係る通信の秘密は侵してはならず、電気通信事業に従事する者は、在職中に知り得た他人の秘密を守る義務を負い、その義務は退職後も継続します。違反には罰則が定められています。本サービスのうち、ノートの共有や通知など利用者どうしのやり取りを媒介する機能については、同条の適用があるものとして取り扱います。 本サービスのどの機能が電気通信事業法の規律の対象となるかは機能の構成によって決まる。{{COMPANY}}の現況と届出の要否は セキュリティ体制 に記載している。 # 第8条（記録の作成及び保存） 委託先は、委託元個人データの取扱状況を確認できるよう、次に掲げる事項に関する記録を作成し、保存するものとする。 委託元個人データへのアクセスの記録（アクセスした者、日時及び操作の種類） 利用権限の付与、変更及び削除の記録 委託元個人データの複製、移送及び削除の記録 再委託先に対する委託元個人データの提供の記録 前項の記録の保存期間は〔 〕年とする。記録の種類により保存期間を異にする場合は、種類ごとの期間を定め、委託元の求めに応じて通知する。 委託先は、委託元の求めに応じ、前項の記録のうち委託元個人データに関する部分の概要を、合理的な範囲で委託元に提供するものとする。ただし、当該提供により委託先の安全管理に支障を及ぼすおそれがある部分については、この限りでない。 委託元個人データの取扱いは個人情報保護法第27条第5項第1号に定める委託に該当するため、同法第29条に基づく第三者提供に係る記録は作成されない。第三者提供に係る記録の開示請求への対応は第11条に定める。 法令 個人情報保護法 第29条（第三者提供に係る記録の作成等） 個人情報取扱事業者が第三者に個人データを提供したときは、原則として提供に関する記録を作成し、保存しなければなりません。ただし、同法第27条第5項各号に該当する提供、すなわち委託、事業承継または共同利用に伴う提供については、記録の作成は不要とされています。本覚書に基づく委託元から委託先への提供はこれに該当するため、第三者提供に係る記録は作成されません。 # 第3章 再委託及び外国にある第三者への提供 # 第9条（再委託） 委託先は、委託元個人データの取扱いの全部または一部を第三者に再委託することができる。再委託を行う場合の承諾の方式は、次のいずれかによるものとし、両当事者は締結時にいずれによるかを合意する。 方式A（個別承諾） 委託先は、再委託を行おうとするときは、あらかじめ、再委託先の名称、所在国、再委託する業務の内容及び再委託先が講ずる安全管理措置の内容を委託元に書面で通知し、委託元の書面による承諾を得るものとする。 方式B（一般承諾及び事前通知） 委託元は、本覚書の締結をもって、別紙3に記載する再委託先への再委託をあらかじめ承諾する。委託先は、再委託先を追加し、または変更しようとするときは、変更の〔 〕日前までに、別紙3を更新したうえで委託元に通知するものとする。 前項方式Bによる場合、委託元は、通知を受けた日から〔 〕日以内に、個人データの保護に関する合理的な理由を示して、書面により当該追加または変更に異議を述べることができる。当該期間内に異議が述べられなかったときは、委託元は当該追加または変更を承諾したものとみなす。 委託元が前項の異議を述べた場合、委託先は、当該異議の理由を検討し、委託元の懸念を解消するために商業的に合理的な努力を行うものとする。委託先が代替となる再委託先を提供できず、かつ委託元の懸念が解消されない場合、委託元は、影響を受ける本サービスの範囲について、違約金を負担することなく本契約を解約することができる。 委託元は、一部の再委託先が本サービスの提供に不可欠であり、当該再委託先の利用に異議を述べた場合には本サービスの全部または一部を利用できなくなる場合があることを了承する。 委託先は、再委託先との間で、本覚書に定める委託先の義務と同等以上の義務を再委託先に課す内容の契約を書面により締結するものとする。当該契約には、少なくとも次の事項を含めるものとする。 委託された業務の範囲を超える取扱いの禁止 安全管理措置の内容 従業者の監督及び秘密保持 漏えい等が発生した場合の委託先に対する通知 再々委託を行う場合の条件 契約終了時の返還または消去 委託先は、再委託先における委託元個人データの取扱状況を定期的に把握し、必要に応じて是正を求めるものとする。 委託先は、再委託先の作為または不作為について、委託先自らが行ったものとして委託元に対する責任を負う。 法令 個人情報保護法 第25条（委託先の監督） 個人情報取扱事業者は、個人データの取扱いの全部または一部を委託する場合、取扱いを委託された個人データの安全管理が図られるよう、委託を受けた者に対する必要かつ適切な監督を行わなければなりません。ガイドライン（通則編）は、監督の内容として、適切な委託先の選定、委託契約の締結、委託先における個人データの取扱状況の把握の3点を挙げ、委託先が再委託を行う場合についても、委託元は再委託の相手方、再委託する業務内容及び再委託先の個人データの取扱方法等を、委託先から報告を受けるなどして把握したうえで適切に監督することが求められるとしています。第9条第1項及び第6項は、この把握を可能にするための定めです。 承諾方式の選択について 方式A（個別承諾）は委託元の統制が強い一方、再委託先の変更のたびに承諾手続が必要となり、サービスの提供に遅れが生じます。方式B（一般承諾と事前通知、異議権）はクラウドサービスで一般的な方式ですが、別紙3の一覧を常に最新に保つ運用が前提となります。{{COMPANY}}がどちらを採用するかを決めたうえで、採用しない方式を条文から削除し、別紙3の一覧を掲載する場所（本ヘルプセンターか、専用ページか）を決めてください。 # 第10条（外国にある第三者への提供） 両当事者は、個人情報保護法第28条第1項が個人データの取扱いの委託に伴う提供にも適用され、委託であることを理由として同条の適用が除外されるものではないことを確認する。 委託先は、外国にある再委託先に対して委託元個人データを提供する場合には、次のいずれかの要件を満たす場合に限り、これを行うものとする。 同等水準国への提供 当該外国が、我が国と同等の水準にあると認められる個人情報の保護に関する制度を有している外国として個人情報保護委員会規則で定めるものである場合 基準適合体制の整備 当該再委託先が、個人情報保護委員会規則で定める基準に適合する体制を整備している者である場合 本人の同意 委託元が、あらかじめ本人から外国にある第三者への提供を認める旨の同意を得ている場合 委託先は、前項の基準に適合する体制を確保するため、外国にある再委託先との間で、個人情報保護法第4章第2節の規定の趣旨に沿った措置の実施を確保する内容の契約を締結するものとする。 委託先は、委託元が自らの立場において個人情報保護法第28条に基づく義務を履行し、及び本人に対する説明を行うことができるよう、委託元の求めに応じ、次に掲げる事項に関する情報を遅滞なく委託元に提供するものとする。 外国にある再委託先の名称 当該再委託先が所在する外国の名称 当該外国における個人情報の保護に関する制度の有無及びその概要（本人の権利利益に重大な影響を及ぼす可能性のある制度の有無を含む。） 当該再委託先に提供する委託元個人データの項目及び提供の頻度 当該再委託先が講ずる個人情報保護法第4章第2節の規定の趣旨に沿った措置（以下「相当措置」という。）の概要 相当措置の実施を確保するために委託先が採用する体制整備の方法 委託先による確認の頻度及び方法 相当措置の実施に支障が生じた場合には、その旨及びその概要 委託先は、外国にある再委託先による相当措置の実施状況及び当該外国における個人情報の保護に関する制度の有無並びにその内容を、少なくとも年1回定期的に確認するものとする。 委託先は、前項の確認の結果、相当措置の実施に支障が生じていることを把握した場合には、必要かつ適切な措置を講じるものとし、相当措置の継続的な実施の確保が困難となったときは、当該再委託先に対する委託元個人データの提供を停止するものとする。この場合、委託先は遅滞なくその旨を委託元に通知する。 委託先は、本人から委託元に対して個人情報保護法第28条第3項に基づく情報提供の求めがあった場合、委託元が当該求めに応じることができるよう、第4項に掲げる事項について必要な情報を遅滞なく提供するものとする。 委託元が第2項の本人の同意による方法を選択する場合、委託先は、委託元が同意の取得に際して本人に提供すべき事項（移転先の外国の名称、当該外国における個人情報の保護に関する制度に関する情報及び当該再委託先が講ずる措置に関する情報）を委託元に提供するものとする。 委託先は、外国にある再委託先を追加し、または変更する場合には、第9条に定める手続に加え、第4項に掲げる事項を委託元に通知するものとする。 法令 個人情報保護法 第28条第1項から第3項（外国にある第三者への提供の制限） 外国にある第三者に個人データを提供する場合には、原則としてあらかじめ本人の同意を得なければなりません。同意によらない場合は、当該外国が、我が国と同等の水準にあると認められる個人情報の保護に関する制度を有している外国として個人情報保護委員会規則で定めるものであるか、または当該第三者が同規則で定める基準に適合する体制を整備している必要があります。同条第1項が適用を除外しているのは同法第27条第1項各号に掲げる場合であり、委託・事業承継・共同利用を定める同条第5項各号は除外されていません。したがって、委託であっても、相手方が外国にある第三者であれば同法第28条が適用されます。同条第3項は、基準適合体制による場合に、相当措置の継続的な実施を確保するために必要な措置を講じ、本人の求めに応じて当該措置に関する情報を提供することを求めています。 法令 個人情報保護法施行規則 第16条（基準適合体制）／第17条第2項（同意取得時の情報提供）／第18条第1項及び第3項（相当措置の継続的な実施の確保） 規則第16条は、基準適合体制として、適切かつ合理的な方法により個人情報保護法第4章第2節の規定の趣旨に沿った措置の実施が確保されていること、または国際的な枠組みに基づく認定を受けていることを定めています。規則第17条第2項は、本人の同意を得る場合に提供すべき事項として、移転先の外国の名称、当該外国の制度に関する情報及び当該第三者が講ずる措置に関する情報の3つを挙げています。規則第18条第1項は、相当措置の実施状況及び当該外国の制度を定期的に確認し、支障があるときは必要な措置を講じ、継続的な実施の確保が困難となったときは提供を停止することを求めています。同条第3項は、本人の求めに応じて提供すべき7つの事項を定めています。第10条第4項から第7項は、委託元がこれらの義務を履行できるようにするための情報提供を定めたものです。 現在、我が国と同等の水準にあると認められる個人情報の保護に関する制度を有している外国として個人情報保護委員会規則で定められているのは、欧州連合（英国を除く。）及び英国です。これら以外の国に所在する再委託先に委託元個人データを提供する場合は、第10条第2項の基準適合体制の整備または本人の同意のいずれかの要件を満たす必要があります。指定の状況は変わることがあるため、締結の前に個人情報保護委員会の公表内容をご確認ください。 実際にどの国のどの事業者に委託元個人データが提供されるかは別紙3に定める。委託元向けの説明は セキュリティ・プライバシーに関するFAQ に、本人向けの説明は プライバシーポリシー の「外国にある第三者への提供」に掲載している。 # 第4章 本人への対応及び漏えい等への対応 # 第11条（本人からの請求等への対応） 本人から個人情報保護法第33条から第35条までに基づく請求（保有個人データの開示、第三者提供に係る記録の開示、内容の訂正、追加または削除、利用の停止、消去及び第三者への提供の停止の請求をいう。以下「開示等の請求等」という。）を受けた場合、及び個人情報の取扱いに関する苦情（同法第40条）の申出を受けた場合の対応は、委託元が行うものとする。 委託先は、委託元が開示等の請求等に応じるために必要となる情報の抽出、複製、訂正、削除その他の作業について、委託元の求めに応じて合理的な範囲で協力するものとする。委託先は、当該協力を、委託元の求めを受けた日から〔 〕営業日以内に完了するよう努めるものとする。 委託先は、委託元個人データに関して本人から直接開示等の請求等または苦情の申出を受けた場合、自らこれに応答せず、当該本人に対して委託元に申し出るよう案内するとともに、法令上禁止されている場合を除き、遅滞なくその旨を委託元に通知するものとする。ただし、委託元の書面による指示がある場合または法令により対応が義務づけられる場合はこの限りでない。 委託元個人データの取扱いは委託に該当し、第三者提供には該当しないため、個人情報保護法第29条に基づく第三者提供に係る記録は作成されない。本人から第三者提供に係る記録の開示を請求された場合、委託元は、該当する記録が存在しない旨を遅滞なく本人に通知するものとする。 委託先は、本サービスにおいて、委託元個人データを含むノート、文字起こしその他のデータを電磁的記録の形式で出力する機能を提供する。委託元は、当該機能を利用して開示の請求に対応することができる。 第2項の協力が委託先にとって過大な作業を伴う場合、両当事者は、当該協力に要する費用の負担について別途協議するものとする。 法令 個人情報保護法 第33条第1項（開示）／第33条第5項（開示）／第34条（訂正等）／第35条第5項（利用停止等）／第38条第1項（手数料）／第40条（苦情の処理） 本人は、保有個人データの開示を、電磁的記録の提供による方法その他の個人情報保護委員会規則で定める方法により請求することができ、第三者提供に係る記録についても開示を請求することができます。同法第34条は内容の訂正、追加または削除の請求を、同法第35条第5項は、当該個人データを利用する必要がなくなった場合、漏えい等の事態が生じた場合その他本人の権利または正当な利益が害されるおそれがある場合における利用停止等の請求を定めています。手数料を徴収できるのは利用目的の通知と開示の請求に限られ、訂正等及び利用停止等の請求については徴収できません。同法第40条は、個人情報取扱事業者に対し、個人情報の取扱いに関する苦情の適切かつ迅速な処理と、そのための体制の整備に努めることを求めています。 対応期限について 第11条第2項の営業日数は、{{COMPANY}}のサポート体制に合わせて記入してください。本人からの請求に対して委託元が回答すべき期限は法令上明示されていませんが、委託元は「遅滞なく」対応する必要があるため、委託先の協力期限はそれより短く設定するのが実務上の目安です。 プライバシーポリシー 第10節に回答までの目安日数を掲げる場合は、その日数と矛盾しない値にしてください。 # 第12条（漏えい等が発生した場合の対応） 委託先は、委託元個人データについて漏えい等が発生し、または発生したおそれがあることを知ったときは、速やかに、遅くとも当該事実を知った時から〔 〕時間以内に、委託元に通知するものとする。 前項の通知には、その時点で把握している範囲で、次に掲げる事項を含めるものとする。把握できていない事項がある場合、委託先は、判明次第、速やかに追加の報告を行う。 漏えい等が発生し、または発生したおそれがある事態の概要 漏えい等が発生し、または発生したおそれがある委託元個人データの項目 漏えい等が発生し、または発生したおそれがある委託元個人データに係る本人の数 原因 二次被害またはそのおそれの有無及びその内容 本人への対応の実施状況 公表の実施状況 再発防止のための措置 その他参考となる事項 委託先は、漏えい等の事態の拡大防止、原因の調査及び復旧のために必要な措置を速やかに講じ、その経過及び結果を委託元に報告するものとする。 委託元個人データに関する個人情報保護委員会への報告（速報及び確報）並びに本人への通知は、委託元が行うものとする。委託先による第1項の通知は、個人情報保護法第26条第1項ただし書に基づく委託元への通知として行われる。 前項にかかわらず、両当事者が書面により合意した場合には、委託先が委託元に代わって個人情報保護委員会への報告及び本人への通知を行うことができる。この場合、委託先は、報告及び通知の内容についてあらかじめ委託元の確認を得るものとする。 委託先は、委託元が個人情報保護委員会への報告及び本人への通知を行うために必要な情報を、委託元の求めに応じて遅滞なく提供するものとする。 両当事者は、漏えい等の事態について外部に公表しようとする場合、法令に基づき公表が義務づけられる場合及び緊急を要する場合を除き、公表の時期、内容及び方法についてあらかじめ相手方と協議するものとする。 本条に基づく通知、報告及び協力は、当該事態について委託先が責任を認めたことを意味するものではない。 法令 個人情報保護法 第26条第1項ただし書（漏えい等の報告等）／同法施行規則 第7条（個人の権利利益を害するおそれが大きいもの）・第8条（個人情報保護委員会への報告）・第10条（本人に対する通知） 個人データの漏えい等であって個人の権利利益を害するおそれが大きいものが生じたときは、個人情報保護委員会への報告と本人への通知が必要です。報告の対象となるのは、要配慮個人情報が含まれる場合、財産的被害が生じるおそれがある場合、不正の目的をもって行われたおそれがある行為による場合、及び本人の数が1,000人を超える場合の4類型で、いずれも発生したおそれがある事態を含みます。報告は、事態を知った後速やかに行う速報と、知った日から30日以内（不正の目的をもって行われたおそれがある行為による場合は60日以内）に行う確報の2段階です。個人データの取扱いの委託を受けた者が、当該事態が生じた旨を委託元に通知したときは、委託先自身の報告義務は免除されます。ガイドライン（通則編）は、速報における「速やかに」の目安をおおむね3日から5日以内としています。 通知期限の設定について 第12条第1項の時間数は、{{COMPANY}}のインシデント対応体制に合わせて記入してください。委託元が個人情報保護委員会への速報を「速やかに」（ガイドラインの目安としておおむね3日から5日以内）

policies/privacy-policy.title: Privacy policy
policies/privacy-policy.description: What information we collect, what we use it for, provision to third parties, cross-border transfers, and how we respond to requests.
policies/privacy-policy.html:
{{COMPANY}} (“we”) handles the personal information it collects in providing {{PRODUCT}} in accordance with the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (“the Act”) and other legislation. This policy sets out what information we collect and how, what we use it for, who we give it to, how long we keep it, and how we respond to requests from individuals.

Security and privacy FAQSupplements this policy in question-and-answer form→Data processing addendum (DPA)The terms of entrustment between corporate customers and us→Terms of serviceWhere the user's own responsibility lies→Automatic transcript deletionHow to set a retention period→
Note

This policy has 19 sections. What we collect and what we use it for are in Sections 2 and 3; the security measures we take are in Section 5; entrustment and sub-processing in Section 6; transfers outside Japan in Section 8; retention and deletion in Section 9; and how to make a request in Section 10. The terms of entrustment between corporate customers and us are set out separately in the data processing addendum (DPA).

#1. Introduction

We handle personal information in accordance with this policy, as a personal information handling business operator under the Act.

This policy covers the personal information we handle in providing the {{PRODUCT}} desktop app (macOS and Windows), the browser extensions, the web version, the API, integrations with external services and the website published at {{DOMAIN}} (together, “the service”). Recording and transcribing meetings is done in the desktop app; the web version only allows viewing and editing notes that have already been created. It covers users with a service account, members of workspaces, people who took part in meetings a user recorded, people who have contacted us, and visitors to our website.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 2, paragraph 1 (definitions)

“Personal information” means information about a living individual that can identify a specific individual by name, date of birth or other description (including anything expressed by voice, movement or other means). It includes information that can readily be collated with other information and thereby identify a specific individual. Recorded meeting audio, transcribed text, AI-generated notes and speaker names can readily be collated with participants' names and calendar invitations, so they are normally personal information.

In the service we hold this information in a form searchable per workspace. Much of what we handle is therefore “personal data” under the Act.

#Our two capacities

In the service we act in two different capacities. That distinction governs how each section of this policy should be read.

Capacity When it applies The position under the Act
Where we handle data in our own right Creating and managing accounts, billing, responding to enquiries, running the website We handle it as a personal information handling business operator, within the purposes of use set out in this policy
Where we handle data entrusted to us by a customer Meeting audio, transcripts, notes and uploaded material held in a workspace on a business plan The contracting company is the controller and we are the processor. We do not process beyond the work entrusted (Section 6)

For data held on a business plan, it is the contracting company that decides on disclosure and deletion. Data in that category may be treated as not being our “retained personal data”, and requests from individuals should as a rule be made to the company they belong to (Section 10).

#2. Information we collect

The information we collect is set out by category below. The “collected directly from the individual” column indicates whether the information is provided by the individual themselves or reaches us by another route, through a user's actions.

Category Examples How it is collected Collected directly from the individual
Account information Name, email address, profile picture, organisation, job title, credentials Entered on the registration screen, or through single sign-on (SSO) Collected directly
Calendar information Meeting titles, start and end times, descriptions, and the names and email addresses of organisers and participants Retrieved from the calendar service the user has connected Organisers' and participants' information is not collected directly
Meeting audio The meeting audio playing on the computer, and audio from the microphone Captured by the desktop app on the user's computer (no recording bot joins the meeting) Not collected directly where the speaker is someone other than the user
Transcripts Text generated from the audio, speaker labels, and the times of utterances Generated automatically from the audio As above
Notes Notes typed by users, AI-formatted notes, summaries and action items Entered by the user and generated by AI The parts derived from what was said in the meeting are not collected directly
Uploaded material Meeting material, images, screenshots and other files Uploaded by the user Not collected directly where the material contains third parties' information
Chat records What is entered into chat, the responses generated, and voice input Through the user's actions Collected directly
Payment information Card type, last four digits of the card number, expiry date, and the billing name, address and contact Collected through our payment provider Collected directly
Device information and logs IP address, the approximate region inferred from it, computer identifier, operating system and version, browser type, desktop app version, the names of other apps using the microphone, crash logs and operation logs Collected automatically through use of the desktop app, the browser extensions and the web version. We do not collect satellite positioning data Collected directly
Usage Screens viewed, how often features are used, referring pages, and connection state Collected automatically using cookies and the like on the web version and our website (Section 13), and from desktop app operation logs Collected directly
Enquiries The body of enquiry emails, attachments, and records of how they were handled Sent to us by the user Collected directly
Information received from integrations Authentication tokens, account identifiers at the integration, and meeting and contact information retrieved from it Retrieved from external services the user has authorised Third parties' information registered at the integration is not collected directly

#Other people's information is included

Meeting audio, transcripts and notes contain not only the personal information of the user operating the service but the personal information of the other people who took part in that meeting. That includes names, organisations, contact details, what they said in the course of business, and their voices themselves. The same goes for calendar information: the names and email addresses of participants in an invitation reach us not from those participants but through the user who connected the calendar.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 20, paragraph 1 (proper acquisition) / Article 21 (notifying the purpose of use on acquisition)

Personal information must not be acquired by deception or other improper means, and unless the purpose of use has been published in advance, it must be notified to the individual or published promptly after acquisition. Recording and transcribing without telling participants risks being “improper means” under Article 20, paragraph 1.

Note

Before you start recording a meeting, tell the participants that it is being recorded and transcribed. The service has a feature that displays on screen that recording is under way, but we recommend telling people in advance as well, orally or in writing. Telling participants is a matter for the user, or the organisation the user belongs to. Sample wording is published in How far you can go with AI minutes (a guide for teams).

#3. Purposes of use

In accordance with Article 17, paragraph 1 of the Act, we specify the purposes of use as far as possible and handle personal information within the scope necessary to achieve them.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 17, paragraph 1 and Article 18, paragraph 1 (specifying the purpose of use / restriction by purpose of use)

The purpose of use must be specified as far as possible, and handling personal information beyond the scope necessary to achieve the specified purpose requires the individual's prior consent. The guidelines give “for use in our business activities” and “for use in marketing activities” as examples of statements that are not specific enough.

We use personal information for the following purposes.

  1. Creating, authenticating, maintaining, changing and deleting accounts
  2. Transcribing meeting audio and generating notes, summaries and action items
  3. Connecting to your calendar, detecting the start of meetings, and bringing together information ahead of a meeting
  4. Sharing notes within the scope the user specifies, and making them searchable within a workspace
  5. Sending data on the user's instruction through integrations with external services the user has enabled
  6. Generating answers to users' questions in the chat feature
  7. Billing, payment, issuing qualified invoices, and dealing with non-payment
  8. Responding to enquiries, bug reports and communications about the contract
  9. Monitoring the availability of the service, investigating the causes of faults, and detecting and preventing misuse and unauthorised access
  10. Analysing how the service is used, in order to improve features and develop new ones
  11. Training AI models and evaluating their accuracy (only where the user or an administrator has permitted this in the settings — see “Use for training AI models” in this section)
  12. Sending announcements about new features, maintenance, changes to the terms and the like
  13. Sending information about the service and related services (we stop where you ask us to)
  14. Responding to requirements of law or of government agencies, and exercising rights or dealing with disputes

Of the above, meeting audio, transcripts, notes and uploaded material held in a workspace on a business plan are handled only within the work entrusted to us by the contracting company. Because a processor cannot handle personal data other than for the work entrusted, we never decide on our own initiative to use a contracting company's data for a different purpose.

#Use for training AI models

Training AI models is different in kind from the processing that makes the service work, so it is stated as a separate purpose of use.

  • On the free and personal plans, data is used for training by default. Users can turn this off at any time under Settings → Preferences → Data and sharing.
  • On business plans (Team and Enterprise), data is not used for training. Because it would go beyond the scope of the entrustment, it is off by default and there is no setting for users to enable it. Administrators can check the setting for the whole workspace.
  • Even where data is used for training, it is processed so that no specific individual can be identified.
  • A change to the setting applies to data created after the change. Data already incorporated into training cannot be removed afterwards.
  • Where we engage an external supplier for transcription or summary generation, we provide in our contract that the data sent will not be used for that supplier's machine learning.

Where the setting is and how to change it are covered in AI models and training data.

Note that Article 30-4 of the Copyright Act permits, within limits, use not aimed at enjoying the thoughts or feelings expressed in a work (including use for information analysis), but that article has a proviso excluding cases that would unreasonably prejudice the copyright holder's interests. We do not rely on what the Copyright Act permits as the basis for training: on the free and personal plans we follow the user's own setting, and on business plans we do not use data for training because it would go beyond the scope of the entrustment.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 19 (prohibition of improper use)

Personal information must not be used in a way that may encourage or induce unlawful or improper acts. Using records obtained through the service on an ongoing basis to monitor particular employees or as material for performance reviews risks running into this provision and into workers' privacy.

#4. Sensitive personal information

Meetings can touch on matters that need careful handling — someone's health, their creed, where they come from, past disputes.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 2, paragraph 3 (definitions) / Article 20, paragraph 2 (proper acquisition) / Enforcement Order Article 2 / Enforcement Rules Article 5

“Sensitive personal information” means personal information including descriptions of the individual's race, creed, social status, medical history, criminal record, the fact of having suffered harm from a crime, and the other matters prescribed by Cabinet Order as requiring particular care in handling so as to avoid unfair discrimination, prejudice or other disadvantage. The Order prescribes the existence of a physical, intellectual, mental or other disability; the results of a health check or other examination; that guidance, medical treatment or dispensing has been carried out by a doctor or similar; that criminal proceedings have been taken; and that juvenile protection proceedings have been taken. Sensitive personal information must not be acquired without the individual's prior consent, save in the cases listed in the items of Article 20, paragraph 2, such as where the law requires it.

Our position is as follows.

  • We do not provide the service for the purpose of actively collecting sensitive personal information.
  • Where someone says in a meeting that “so-and-so is undergoing treatment”, and that remains in the transcript, that part may be sensitive personal information as a medical history. A conjectural remark such as “they seem unwell”, on the other hand, is not sensitive personal information.
  • The person whose consent is needed for acquiring sensitive personal information is the speaker whose information it is. The consent of a workspace administrator or a meeting organiser cannot stand in their place.
  • For meetings where sensitive personal information may be discussed, do not start recording, or pause recording at the point concerned. You can also delete the relevant section after recording.

A breach of personal data containing sensitive personal information is reportable to the Personal Information Protection Commission even where only one person is affected (Enforcement Rules Article 7, item 1). Where you use the service for work likely to involve sensitive personal information — healthcare, HR, legal — we recommend starting recording meeting by meeting and limiting which meetings you record. How to think about this by sector is covered in Use in healthcare, finance and the professions.

#5. Security measures

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 23 (security control measures) / Article 24 (supervision of staff)

A business must take the necessary and appropriate measures to prevent the leakage, loss or damage of the personal data it handles and otherwise keep it secure, and must exercise the necessary and appropriate supervision over staff who handle personal data.

The measures we take are organised under five headings.

#Organisational security measures

We have rules on the handling of personal data, with the staff who handle it and the person responsible clearly identified. Access records are collected and reviewed periodically so that how data is handled can be established. Reporting lines for a breach are set in advance, and the rules are kept under continuous review.

#Personnel security measures

We have confidentiality arrangements with our staff and provide training on personal data protection when they join and periodically thereafter. Staff involved in running the service are required not to view customers' data beyond what their work requires.

#Physical security measures

Servers handling personal data are housed in data centres with entry control and monitoring. Work devices have disk encryption and screen locking applied, and procedures are set for taking equipment and electronic media off site.

#Technical security measures

Access rights are limited to what work requires, with authentication in place. Personal data is encrypted at rest and in transit. To prevent unauthorised access from outside we separate networks, restrict traffic and detect anomalous behaviour, and we monitor vulnerability information continuously and apply fixes.

#Understanding the external environment

Where we handle personal data in a foreign country, we establish that country's personal data protection regime (including any regime on government access to data) and take measures such as encryption in transit and at rest, limits on retention, and contractual provision that data entered will not be used for anything other than generating the response. The regions data is stored in, the destination countries, the route we use to comply with Article 28 of the Act, and what information we provide at an individual's request are gathered in Section 8.

Matters whose publication would itself risk prejudicing security — the specific method of access control, the detail of measures preventing unauthorised access and the like — are left out of the above (the parenthesis in Article 10, item 1 of the Enforcement Order).

A fuller explanation of each heading is published in Our security arrangements. Which certifications and third-party assessments we hold (ISMS certification, the Privacy Mark, a SOC 2 Type II report and so on) is set out in the table on that page; this policy does not list them individually.

Editorial note

Replace the five headings above with the measures {{COMPANY}} actually takes. Where something can be stated specifically — where the data centres are, what encryption is used, how permissions are managed, how long logs are kept, how often vulnerabilities are addressed — it is better stated specifically, because it can then be used in processor due-diligence reviews. Make sure what is written here does not conflict with the corresponding sections of Our security arrangements.

#6. Entrustment

We may entrust the handling of personal data to others within the scope necessary to achieve the purposes of use, and we are also entrusted with handling data by corporate customers. Both directions are explained separately.

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 25 (supervision of processors) / Article 27, paragraph 5, item 1

Where personal data is provided in connection with entrustment, the recipient is not a third party. The controller, on the other hand, must exercise the necessary and appropriate supervision over the party entrusted so that the personal data is kept secure. The guidelines identify three elements of that supervision: selecting an appropriate processor, concluding a contract with it, and keeping informed of how it handles the personal data. The same applies to sub-processing.

#Where we act as your processor

On business plans, the contracting company is the controller and we are the processor. The service is designed to turn the content of audio into text and to summarise that content with AI, which presupposes that we handle the content of the personal data. That is what distinguishes it from external storage services, which work on the basis of a contractual undertaking not to handle the data stored.

Within that arrangement, we do not process personal data beyond the work entrusted. As part of supervising their processor under Article 25 of the Act, we recommend that contracting companies review the measures we describe in this policy and in the data processing addendum (DPA).

#Where we sub-process

In order to provide the service, we sub-process the handling of personal data to suppliers of the following kinds. In each case we have selection criteria, conclude a contract, and keep ourselves informed of how they handle data.

Kind of sub-processor Work entrusted Information handled
Cloud infrastructure providers Providing servers and storage All information handled in the service
Speech recognition and generative AI providers Producing transcripts, generating notes and summaries, generating chat answers Meeting audio, transcripts, notes, uploaded material, chat input
Payment providers Processing payments and issuing invoices Payment information and billing details
Customer support platform providers Receiving enquiries and managing the history of responses The content of enquiries, and account information
Analytics and fault detection providers Analysing usage and detecting defects Device information, logs and usage
Email delivery providers Sending announcements and notifications Names and email addresses
Editorial note

State the actual names of sub-processors, the countries they are in and the substance of the contractual arrangements, to match {{COMPANY}}'s actual relationships. Where suppliers are named, check that the contract allows naming them. Where a processor is outside Japan, list the same supplier in the table in Section 8 and in Schedule 3 of the data processing addendum (DPA), and make sure all three agree.

#7. Provision to third parties

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 27, paragraph 1 (restriction on provision to third parties)

Providing personal data to a third party requires the individual's prior consent, save in the cases listed in the items of that paragraph — where the law requires it, where it is necessary to protect life, limb or property and obtaining consent is difficult, and so on.

We do not provide customers' personal data to third parties except in the following cases.

  • Where the individual has consented
  • Where the law requires it
  • Where it is necessary to protect someone's life, limb or property and obtaining the individual's consent is difficult
  • Where it is particularly necessary for improving public health or promoting the sound growth of children and obtaining the individual's consent is difficult
  • Where it is necessary to cooperate with a national or local government body, or someone they have engaged, in performing duties prescribed by law, and obtaining the individual's consent would risk impeding those duties
  • Where personal data is provided in connection with a business succession following a merger or otherwise (Article 27, paragraph 5, item 2 of the Act)

We do not provide personal data to third parties by the opt-out method under Article 27, paragraph 2 of the Act. Nor do we sell personal data.

Note that provision in connection with entrustment described in Section 6, and provision in connection with a business succession, are not provision to a third party by virtue of Article 27, paragraph 5 of the Act. We do not currently handle personal data under a joint use framework (item 3 of that paragraph).

#Where a user's own action sends data to an external service

The service has integrations that send notes and transcripts to external services. Where such an integration is enabled and data is sent, the destination is another business, not a processor of ours.

Note

Sending data to an integration can amount to provision to a third party under the Act where it contains personal data. The lawfulness of that provision has to be secured by the personal information handling business operator that carried out the integration — usually the company the user belongs to. Where the integration is with a business outside Japan, that business deals with it in its own capacity as provision to a third party in a foreign country under Article 28 of the Act (Section 8). Before enabling an integration, check that it is within your organisation's rules on handling personal information and within the purposes of use you have specified. Disconnecting an integration does not remove data already sent to it; delete it in that service.

The same goes for issuing share links outside a workspace: note that who can view the material then extends beyond your organisation. How to set sharing is covered in Controlling sharing, and the services you can integrate with in List of integrations.

#Records of provision to third parties

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 29 (creating records of provision to third parties)

Where personal data is provided to a third party a record must be created and kept, but no record is needed for provision falling within the items of Article 27, paragraph 1 or the items of paragraph 5 of that article.

The personal data we handle on business plans is handled in connection with entrustment and is not provision to a third party, so no record of provision to a third party is created for it. Where you request disclosure of records of provision to third parties and there is no such record, we tell you so without delay.

#8. Provision to third parties in foreign countries

Data in the service is, as a rule, stored in a region within Japan. Some processing, such as transcription and summary generation, may however be entrusted to suppliers outside Japan, in which case personal data is transferred abroad. This section covers those transfers, which we make in order to provide the service. Data sent to an integration by a user's own action is treated as provision to a third party in a foreign country by the business that carried out the integration (Section 7).

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 28, paragraph 1 (restriction on provision to third parties in foreign countries)

Where a personal information handling business operator provides personal data to a third party in a foreign country (other than a country designated by rules of the Personal Information Protection Commission as having a personal data protection regime of a standard equivalent to Japan's) and that third party does not have in place a framework meeting the standards set by those rules, it must, save in the cases listed in the items of Article 27, paragraph 1, obtain the individual's prior consent to provision to a third party in a foreign country.

#It applies to entrustment too

What Article 28, paragraph 1 excludes are the items of paragraph 1 of Article 27; the items of paragraph 5 of Article 27, covering entrustment, business succession and joint use, are not excluded. The reasoning that domestic entrustment is not provision to a third party does not carry over where the counterparty is a third party in a foreign country. An arrangement that entrusts transcription or summary generation to a supplier outside Japan is squarely within Article 28.

What matters is not where the data is stored but whether personal data is provided to a third party in a foreign country. Having servers in Japan is not a reason for saying there is no provision abroad. Sending data to an external supplier for inference can amount to such “provision”.

#The three routes, and the one we use

There are three ways of complying with Article 28, and we use the second.

Route What it involves Whether we use it
Provision to a country with an equivalent regime Provision to a supplier in a country designated by rules as having a regime of a standard equivalent to Japan's. Only the EU (excluding the UK) and the UK are designated; the United States is not Where the destination is in such a country, this is the basis used
Provision to a party with an adequate framework in place Provision to a supplier with a framework meeting the standards in Rule 16 of the Personal Information Protection Commission's rules (implementation of measures in line with the intent of Chapter 4, Section 2 of the Act ensured by appropriate and reasonable means, or certification under an international framework) This is the route we use
Provision with the individual's consent Obtaining the individual's prior consent to the transfer. When obtaining consent, the name of the country, information on that country's regime and information on the measures the recipient takes must be provided (Article 28, paragraph 2 of the Act and Rule 17, paragraph 2) Obtaining individual consent from every meeting participant is impracticable, so as a rule we do not use it

Meeting records contain the personal information of participants who do not have an account. Since obtaining individual consent to a cross-border transfer from all of them is not realistic, we use the route of ensuring implementation of equivalent measures by contract (the adequate-framework route). Specifically, we conclude contracts with recipient suppliers ensuring the implementation of measures in line with the intent of Chapter 4, Section 2 of the Act, and provide personal data only to suppliers with that framework in place.

#What we do on an ongoing basis

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 28, paragraph 3 / Enforcement Rules Article 18, paragraphs 1 and 3

A business that has provided personal data to a party with an adequate framework in place must take the measures necessary to ensure continued implementation of the equivalent measures, and must provide information about those necessary measures at an individual's request. Rule 18, paragraph 1 requires periodic verification of the implementation of the equivalent measures and of whether the foreign country has a regime and what it contains; the taking of necessary and appropriate measures where an impediment to implementation arises; and the cessation of provision where continued implementation becomes difficult to ensure. Paragraph 3 of that rule lists seven matters to be provided at an individual's request: an outline of the measures taken to ensure implementation of the equivalent measures, an outline of the equivalent measures the recipient takes, how often and by what means verification is carried out, the name of the country, whether that country has a regime and an outline of it, an outline of any impediment to implementation, and an outline of the measures taken about it.

We do three things.

  1. We verify periodically how recipient suppliers are implementing the equivalent measures, and the personal data protection regime of the destination country (including any regime on government access to data).
  2. Where an impediment to the implementation of the equivalent measures arises, we take the necessary and appropriate measures.
  3. Where continued implementation of the equivalent measures becomes difficult to ensure, we stop providing personal data to that supplier.

At an individual's request, we provide information on the seven matters set out in Rule 18, paragraph 3. We are not required to publish these at all times, but we answer requests without delay. Please contact us at the address in Section 17.

#Publishing information about the destination country's regime

Separately from providing information at an individual's request, where personal data is handled in a foreign country, the measures taken in light of an understanding of that country's regime must be kept in a state where individuals can know them, as one of the matters published about retained personal data (Article 32, paragraph 1, item 4 of the Act and Article 10, item 1 of the Enforcement Order). These are two distinct obligations, and we meet both.

The third parties in foreign countries to which we currently provide personal data are as follows.

Kind of recipient Country Categories of information provided Purpose of provision Measures we take
[kind of supplier, or name] [country, and the country the servers are in] [categories of information provided] [purpose of provision] [measures taken in light of an understanding of that country's regime]
Editorial note

This table provides only the frame. Fill in the [ ] to match {{COMPANY}}'s actual relationships, and do not put in placeholder supplier names or countries that do not exist. Where the country the servers are in cannot be identified for some item, state that it cannot be identified, why, and any information useful to individuals (Personal Information Protection Commission, “Q&A on the Guidelines”, Q10-25). Keep what you write consistent with the table of sub-processors in Section 6 and with Schedule 3 of the data processing addendum (DPA).

#9. Retention and deletion

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 22 (keeping data accurate etc.)

A business must keep personal data accurate and up to date within the scope necessary to achieve the purpose of use, and must endeavour to erase personal data without delay once it is no longer needed. It is a duty to endeavour, but keeping records indefinitely without setting a retention period drifts away from its intent.

We set a retention period for each category of data and delete it once that period passes.

Category How the retention period works How it is deleted
Meeting audio Only for as long as is needed to produce the transcript Deleted once transcription is complete. We never keep the meeting audio itself
Transcripts No automatic deletion by default. Where a user or administrator sets a retention period, that period Automatic deletion under the setting, or deletion by the user individually
Notes and summaries While the account is active Deletion by the user individually, or deletion of the account
Uploaded material While the account is active As above
Account information While the account is active, and for a set period after it is closed Deleted once the closure process is complete
Payment and billing records The period the law requires them to be kept Deleted once that period passes
Operation and access logs As long as needed to investigate misuse and respond to faults Deleted once that period passes
Backups As long as needed to recover from a fault Deleted progressively as generations are replaced
Integration authentication tokens While the integration is active Deleted when the integration is disconnected
Editorial note

The retention periods above set out the approach only. State specific numbers of days or months to match {{COMPANY}}'s actual practice. The retention period for account information after closure, the log retention period and how long it takes for data to disappear from backups are asked about particularly often in processor due-diligence reviews. Even where the figures cannot be settled, do not leave out the fact that data remains for a period in recovery backups and audit logs. For payment and billing records, check the tax law obligations on keeping books and records with your finance team. Make the figures you enter consistent with the [ ] in Articles 8 and 15 of the data processing addendum (DPA).

Automatic transcript deletion is off by default (no automatic deletion). Where it is enabled, the retention period can be set to 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months or 1 year. How to configure it and what remains after deletion are covered in Automatic transcript deletion, and what remains after an account is deleted in Deleting your account.

Even after data disappears from the screen, it remains for a period in recovery backups and audit logs. What remains in an audit log is a record of who did what and when; it does not include the body of notes or transcripts.

Where data has been used to train an AI model and incorporated into the model's weights, it is not technically possible to extract or remove individual data afterwards. With that in mind, we let you choose by a setting whether data is used for training, and tell you in advance that changing the setting does not apply retrospectively (Section 3).

#10. Requests for disclosure, correction and cessation of use

You may make the following requests in relation to your own retained personal data.

What you are requesting Basis
Notification of the purpose of use Act on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 32, paragraph 2
Disclosure (including disclosure of records of provision to third parties) Article 33, paragraphs 1 and 5
Correction, addition or deletion where the content is not factual Article 34
Cessation of use, or erasure Article 35, paragraph 1
Cessation of provision to third parties Article 35, paragraph 3
LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 33, paragraph 1 (disclosure) / Article 35, paragraph 5 (cessation of use etc.) / Enforcement Rules Article 30

An individual may request disclosure by provision in electromagnetic form or by another method prescribed by rules of the Personal Information Protection Commission. The Rules prescribe provision in electromagnetic form, delivery of a document, and other methods determined by the business. The guidelines state that it is desirable to respond as far as possible in the form the individual wants, including provision in a readable and searchable format and, where technically possible, in a format portable to another business. Article 35, paragraph 5 further provides that cessation of use or erasure may be requested where the personal data is no longer needed, where a situation under the main text of Article 26, paragraph 1 (a breach) has arisen, or where there is otherwise a risk of harm to the individual's rights or legitimate interests.

#How to make a request

  1. Write to {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}} telling us what you are requesting (which of the above it is) and which data it concerns.
  2. To confirm your identity, we ask you to produce the documents we specify. We choose a method that is not unduly burdensome, so far as it lets us match the request to the account information.
  3. We also accept requests from representatives: a statutory representative of a minor or an adult ward, and a representative the individual has appointed (Article 13 of the Enforcement Order). In that case, please enclose documents evidencing the authority.

#How and when we respond

Disclosure is made, as a rule, by provision in electromagnetic form — either a download from the service or an attachment to an email. If you would prefer a document, please say so. We check the position and respond without delay after receiving a request.

Where we cannot meet a request in whole or in part, we endeavour to explain why (Article 36 of the Act). We may be unable to meet a request where we cannot confirm your identity, where doing so would risk harming the rights or interests of others, or where it would breach the law.

#Fees

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 38, paragraphs 1 and 2 (fees)

where notification of the purpose of use is sought or a request for disclosure is received — only then may a fee be charged, within a range recognised as reasonable in light of the actual costs. Requests for correction and for cessation of use are not among those for which a fee may be charged.

We do not charge a fee for requests for correction, addition, deletion, cessation of use, erasure or cessation of provision to third parties. For requests for notification of the purpose of use and for disclosure, we may charge a fee within a reasonable range reflecting the actual costs.

Editorial note

Settle two things to match {{COMPANY}}'s policy. First, the amount of any fee for notification of the purpose of use and for disclosure: where an amount is set it must be published (Article 32, paragraph 1, item 3 of the Act), and where the policy is not to charge, say plainly “we do not charge a fee”. Second, the internal target for responding to requests. The law says only “without delay” and sets no number of days, so where you state a target, state also that it may be extended where identity checks take time or where a large volume of data is involved.

#What you can do yourself

The following can be done in the service without waiting for a request.

  • Exporting notes and transcripts (Exporting notes in bulk)
  • Deleting notes, transcripts and your account (Deleting your account)
  • Changing your name and email address (Account and email address changes)

#If you are on a business plan

For data held in a workspace on a business plan, it is the contracting company that decides on disclosure and deletion. Requests of that kind should as a rule be made to your organisation's privacy contact. Where you approach us directly, we will direct you to your organisation and tell the contracting company that you have been in touch. What assistance we give and by when is set out in Article 11 of the data processing addendum (DPA).

#11. Matters published about retained personal data

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 32, paragraph 1 / Enforcement Order Article 10

A business must keep in a state where individuals can know them (including by answering without delay at an individual's request) the following in relation to retained personal data: the business's name, address and the name of its representative; the purposes of use of all retained personal data; the procedures for responding to access requests (including the amount of any fee set); and the matters prescribed by Cabinet Order. Those prescribed matters are the measures taken for security (excluding those whose being known would risk prejudicing security), where complaints may be made, and the name of any certified personal information protection organisation and where complaints may be made to it.

The statutory disclosures, and where each appears in this policy, are as follows.

Statutory disclosure Basis Where it appears in this policy
The business's name and address, and the name of its representative Article 32, paragraph 1, item 1 Section 17
The purposes of use of all retained personal data Article 32, paragraph 1, item 2 Section 3
Procedures for responding to access requests Article 32, paragraph 1, item 3 Section 10
The amount of any fee set Article 32, paragraph 1, item 3 Section 10
Measures taken for the security of retained personal data Article 32, paragraph 1, item 4 and Enforcement Order Article 10, item 1 Section 5 (including understanding the external environment) and Section 8
Where complaints may be made Enforcement Order Article 10, item 2 Section 17
The name of any certified personal information protection organisation and where complaints may be made to it Enforcement Order Article 10, item 3 Section 17

Where you would like any of the matters in this table that are not set out in this policy to be published, please contact the address in Section 17 and we will answer without delay.

#12. What we do if there is a breach

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 26, paragraphs 1 and 2 (reporting breaches etc.) / Enforcement Rules Articles 7, 8 and 10

Where personal data is leaked, lost or damaged, or there is a risk of that, four categories set out in Rule 7 must be reported to the Personal Information Protection Commission and notified to the individuals concerned: those involving personal data containing sensitive personal information; those involving personal data where there is a risk of financial harm; those arising from an act that may have been carried out with improper intent; and those involving more than 1,000 individuals. Reporting has two stages: a preliminary report promptly after learning of the incident, and a final report within 30 days of learning of it (60 days where the act may have been carried out with improper intent). What must be notified to individuals is an outline of the incident, the categories of personal data involved, the cause, whether there is secondary harm or a risk of it and what it is, and any other relevant matters.

What we do is as follows.

  1. On detecting an incident, we begin investigating immediately and take measures to prevent the harm spreading and to restore the position.
  2. For personal data we handle in our own right, we make the preliminary and final reports to the Personal Information Protection Commission and notify the individuals concerned. Where notifying individuals is difficult, we publish the incident or take other alternative measures necessary to protect individuals' rights and interests.
  3. For personal data we handle as a processor on a business plan, we notify the contracting company as controller promptly after learning of the incident. Where a processor notifies the controller, the processor's own reporting obligation to the Commission falls away (the proviso to Article 26, paragraph 1 of the Act). Reporting to the Commission and notifying individuals are done by the contracting company, and we provide the information needed. The notification deadline and what is reported are set out in Article 12 of the data processing addendum (DPA).
  4. “Promptly” for the preliminary report is indicated by the guidelines as roughly within three to five days. The 30 and 60 days for the final report are deadlines set by the Rules. The two are different in kind, and we keep them distinct in our internal procedures as well.
  5. We publish the outcome of our investigation into the cause and the measures taken to prevent recurrence where appropriate.

Because transcripts can contain sensitive personal information, an incident can be reportable under Rule 7, item 1 even where only one person is affected. With that in mind, we have built measures including encryption at rest into our security design (Section 5).

#13. Cookies and external transmission

This section covers two things: the use of cookies and the like on our website and in the web version, and causing information to be sent from users' computers to businesses other than us (external transmission).

#Use of cookies

We use cookies and similar technologies (“cookies”) on the service's website and in the web version.

Type Purpose If disabled
Essential cookies Keeping you signed in, maintaining security, preventing misuse Basic functionality, including signing in, becomes unavailable
Functional cookies Remembering display language, screen settings, the screen you last had open and the like Settings are not saved and have to be chosen again each time
Analytics cookies Understanding how screens are used, detecting defects, considering improvements You are excluded from usage analysis. Functionality is unaffected
Advertising cookies Delivering advertising and measuring its effect The advertising shown is not based on your usage

Whether cookies are accepted can be changed in your browser settings. Disabling essential cookies prevents you signing in to the service.

#Disclosures concerning external transmission

LegislationTelecommunications Business Act, Article 27-12 (notices concerning instructions to transmit information) / Enforcement Rules Article 22-2-29

A telecommunications carrier, or a person carrying on a category III business, that provides a telecommunications service prescribed by ministerial ordinance must, before instructing a user's device to transmit information, notify the user of, or place where the user can readily learn, the content of the information about the user that will be transmitted, the name of the party that will handle that information using the telecommunications equipment it is sent to, and the purpose for which it will be used. The notice must be in Japanese, in plain language avoiding technical terms, and displayed at an appropriate size without the user having to take any action (Rule 22-2-28).

The information we cause to be sent from users' devices to businesses other than us in connection with use of the service is as follows.

Recipient Information transmitted Purpose of use at the recipient How to stop it
[name of business] [information transmitted] [purpose of use at the recipient] [how a request to stop is received, and what functionality is limited as a result]
Editorial note

This table provides only the frame. Fill in the [ ] with one row for each analytics tag, advertising tag and fault detection mechanism {{COMPANY}} actually embeds. Do not put in placeholder names of businesses that do not exist. Where a means of stopping transmission is offered, state whether it exists, which transmissions it covers, how a request is received, and what functionality is limited as a result (Rule 22-2-31). Where no advertising cookies are used, delete the “advertising cookies” row from the table above; listing functionality that is not used would be inconsistent with what Section 14 says about personal-related information.

Also ask your legal team to confirm whether {{PRODUCT}} is a telecommunications service within Article 27-12 of the Act. Rule 22-2-27 limits it to four categories: services that carry others' communications, services that transmit at the request of unspecified users, search services, and services intended to be viewed by unspecified users. Business SaaS with no messaging between users and no publication to the world at large may fall outside it, but the conclusion turns on the implementation. The result of the same check also affects whether a report to the Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications under Article 28 of that Act is required in the event of a breach (Section 12). Do not write definitively about registration where it has not been confirmed.

Meeting audio, transcribed text and the body of notes are not among the information transmitted externally for the analytics purposes above. They are handled only to the extent needed to provide the service.

#14. Personal-related information

LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 2, paragraph 7 / Article 31, paragraph 1 (restrictions on providing personal-related information to third parties)

“Personal-related information” means information about a living individual that is neither personal information, pseudonymously processed information nor anonymously processed information. Browsing history of an individual collected through a device identifier such as a cookie is given as an example. Where personal-related information is provided to a third party and it is anticipated that the recipient will acquire it as personal data, it must be confirmed in advance that the individual's consent has been obtained by the recipient. Where the recipient is a third party in a foreign country, it must also be confirmed that the individual has been given information on that country's personal data protection regime, on the measures that third party takes and other information useful to them.

Where you browse our website without being signed in, the browsing history we collect through cookies is normally personal-related information as far as we are concerned. Where we provide that information to a third party and it is anticipated that the recipient will acquire it as personal data, we carry out the confirmations above and create a record of them.

Browsing history while signed in to the service, on the other hand, can readily be collated with account information and is therefore personal information as far as we are concerned. In that case Sections 7 and 8 apply. Note that which rules apply changes between being signed out and signed in.

#15. Use by minors

The service is designed for recording meetings at work and is not intended for use by minors.

Terms of service — where someone below the minimum age set there uses the service, they should sign up with the consent of a person with parental authority or another statutory representative. Where we find that we have collected personal information from someone below that age without a statutory representative's consent, we delete it promptly. If you think that may have happened, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}.

Where meeting participants include minors, the user doing the recording and the organisation they belong to need to take the necessary care and obtain consent in relation to those participants' personal information.

#16. Changes to this policy

We may change this policy because of amendments to legislation, changes to the service's features, changes in our processor relationships or other circumstances.

  • The changed version applies from the moment it is published on this page at {{DOMAIN}}.
  • Where we change a purpose of use, we do not change it beyond a scope reasonably recognised as related to the purpose before the change (Article 17, paragraph 2 of the Act). Where we do change it, we notify individuals of the changed purpose or publish it (Article 21, paragraph 3).
  • Where a change significantly affects individuals' rights and obligations, we tell you before it starts to apply, by a notice in the service or by email.
  • Past versions are made available for reference on this page, with the date of each revision.

Note that the Act Partially Amending the Act on the Protection of Personal Information and Related Acts was promulgated on 17 July 2026, and the position may change in future.

Editorial note

State the period of advance notice for significant changes (30 days, for instance) to match {{COMPANY}}'s policy. Where no fixed period is used, leave the wording as “before it starts to apply” and do not state a number of days. Where past versions will not be published, delete the last item. Keep the notice period consistent with the variation procedure in Article 17, paragraph 3 of the data processing addendum (DPA).

#17. How to contact us

Enquiries about this policy and the handling of personal information, access requests and complaints are received at the following.

Item Details
Name of the business {{COMPANY}}
Address {{ADDRESS}}
Name of the representative {{REP}}
Contact for personal information {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}
Where to make a complaint {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}
Personal information protection manager [team and job title]
Certified personal information protection organisation [name and where complaints may be made. Where not a member, “not applicable”]
LegislationAct on the Protection of Personal Information, Article 40 (handling complaints)

A business must endeavour to handle complaints about the handling of personal information appropriately and promptly, and to put in place the arrangements needed to do so.

We check and endeavour to handle appropriately and promptly any complaint we receive. If you are not satisfied with our response, you may make a submission to the Personal Information Protection Commission.

Editorial note

Decide, according to {{COMPANY}}'s policy, whether to publish the personal information protection manager's name or only their team and job title; the law does not require the name to be published. Where you are not a member of a certified personal information protection organisation, write “not applicable” rather than deleting the row (the list of disclosures in Section 11 assumes the row is there). Where enquiries are accepted by telephone, add {{PHONE}}.

#18. For customers outside Japan

This policy is written under Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information. Where you use the service from outside Japan, the law of the country or region you live in may give you rights beyond those set out in this policy. If you wish to exercise such a right, contact {{PRIVACY_EMAIL}}; we will look into it and respond in accordance with the applicable law. For corporate contracts, please also review the terms in the data processing addendum (DPA).
